title: Over a one-dimensional Noetherian local domain, residue field extensions in a finite extension of fraction fields are finite
statement: Let $\varphi:R\to S$ be an injective homomorphism of integral domains, with fraction fields $K$ of $R$ and $L$ of $S$, so that $\varphi$ induces a field extension $K\subseteq L$ [def-pc-field-extension]; assume $\dim_KL<\infty$. Assume $R$ is a Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and Krull dimension $1$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Then (1) every prime ideal $\mathfrak n\subset S$ with $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak n)=\mathfrak m$ is a maximal ideal of $S$; (2) there are only finitely many such prime ideals; (3) for each of them the residue field $\kappa(\mathfrak n)=S_{\mathfrak n}/\mathfrak nS_{\mathfrak n}$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], which is a field extension of $\kappa(\mathfrak m)=R/\mathfrak m$ through $\varphi$, is finite-dimensional over $\kappa(\mathfrak m)$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 031F (lemma-finite-extension-residue-fields-dimension-1, line 29241), statement. Tag verified in tags/tags: 031F,algebra-lemma-finite-extension-residue-fields-dimension-1

proof.text: Since a one-dimensional local domain is not a field, its maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ contains a nonzero element $x$. The injection of fraction fields identifies $S$ with an $R$-submodule of $L$, and a $K$-basis identifies $L$ with $K^{\oplus n}$ for $n=[L:K]$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-dim-one-submodule-quotient-finite-length] to this submodule and $x$; $S/xS$ has finite length as an $R$-module.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 031F (lemma-finite-extension-residue-fields-dimension-1), proof, first two sentences; Lemma Tag 00PE (lemma-finite-length)

proof.text: Because $x\in\mathfrak m$, $xS\subseteq\mathfrak mS$, and the quotient map $q:S/xS\twoheadrightarrow B=S/\mathfrak mS$ is surjective. For any strict chain $U_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq U_a$ of $R$-submodules of $B$, the preimages $q^{-1}(U_i)$ are $R$-submodules of $S/xS$ and remain strict: choose an element of $U_{i+1}\setminus U_i$ and lift it through $q$. Hence $B$ has finite $R$-length [def-weil-pbc-module-length]. The action of $R$ on $B$ factors through the field $k=R/\mathfrak m$, and its $R$-submodules are exactly its $k$-linear subspaces. If $B$ had arbitrarily large $k$-linearly independent families, their successive spans would give arbitrarily long strict chains, contrary to finite length. Thus $B$ is finite-dimensional over $k$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 031F, proof, sentences 3-5; Lemma Tag 00IY (lemma-dimension-is-length)

proof.text: The finite-dimensional $k$-algebra $B$ is Artinian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-dim-algebra-artinian]. More precisely for the prime conclusions, $k$ is a local ring with the sole prime $(0)$ and $B$ is a finite $k$-algebra, so [lem-weil-pbc-finite-over-zero-dim-local-discrete-spectrum] gives finitely many prime ideals of $B$, all maximal. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-quotient-homeomorphism-zero-locus] for $S\to B$, these correspond to the primes $\mathfrak n$ of $S$ containing $\mathfrak m S$, equivalently those with inverse image $\mathfrak m$ under $R\to S$ (the inverse image is a proper ideal containing the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$). A prime $\mathfrak n$ in this correspondence is maximal because $S/\mathfrak n\cong B/\bar{\mathfrak n}$ is a field. If $B=0$, there are no such primes. This proves (1) and (2).

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 031F, proof, sentences 5-7; Lemmas Tags 00J6 and 00JB

proof.text: For a prime $\mathfrak n$ from Step 3, the field $S/\mathfrak n=B/\bar{\mathfrak n}$ is a quotient of the finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $B$, hence has finite $k$-dimension. The field map $k\to S/\mathfrak n$ is injective, because it sends $1$ to $1$. Since $\mathfrak n$ is maximal, every $s\notin\mathfrak n$ has nonzero image and thus becomes a unit in $S/\mathfrak n$; the fraction formula $a/s\mapsto(a\bmod\mathfrak n)/(s\bmod\mathfrak n)$ therefore gives a map $S_{\mathfrak n}\to S/\mathfrak n$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. It is surjective since $a/1\mapsto a\bmod\mathfrak n$, and its kernel is $\mathfrak nS_{\mathfrak n}$ since a fraction maps to zero exactly when its numerator lies in $\mathfrak n$. Thus $S_{\mathfrak n}/\mathfrak nS_{\mathfrak n}\cong S/\mathfrak n$ as $k$-algebras, proving (3).

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 031F, proof, final sentence
